abstract: Non-visual arrestins, {beta}-arrestin 1 ({beta}-arr1) and {beta}-arrestin 2 ({beta}-arr2), regulate GPCR desensitization, internalization, and signaling, making them potentially attractive therapeutic targets in several diseases. However, their high sequence similarity complicates isoform- specific targeting. Their C-tails exhibit considerably lower sequence conservation, but they remain poorly characterized due to their disordered nature, limiting our understanding of how C-tail conformational dynamics influence arrestin structure and function. To address this gap, we investigated how C-tail dynamics shape conformational landscape of non-visual arrestins and their membrane interactions using millisecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Our findings reveal isoform-specific contributions of the arrestin core and C-tail to activation- related motifs, interdomain rotation, and intramolecular communication networks. Notably, C- tail-swapped constructs largely recapitulated the conformational behavior associated with the corresponding C-tail isoform, highlighting the transferable nature of C-tail-encoded dynamic properties. The isoforms also displayed distinct membrane-binding modes: {beta}-arr1 preferentially engaged the membrane through C-domain, whereas {beta}-arr2 used N-domain. C- tail truncation further altered membrane-binding mode of {beta}-arr1, underscoring the regulatory role of the distal tail in membrane engagement. In addition to wild-type proteins, we examined the effects of disease-associated mutations on the C-tail dynamics. {beta}-arr1T224N and {beta}-arr2T268I mutants, reported to co-occur in a lung cancer patient sample in the COSMIC database, induced distinct conformational profiles where the former displayed inactive-like whereas the latter favored active-like dynamics. Overall, our findings highlight C-tail dynamics as a key determinant of isoform-specific arrestin regulation and suggest that disease-associated mutations may reshape arrestin conformational landscapes, potentially affecting their function. These insights may guide the development of isoform- and mutation-specific therapeutic strategies.
